questions.title: The Three Reasons a Spread Exists
questions.prompt: A stock trades with a bid of $49.98 and an ask of $50.02. Why isn't that spread just $0.00 if the market maker truly believes the stock is worth $50.00? Name the three distinct risks the spread is compensating the market maker for.
questions.modelAnswer: The bid-ask spread compensates a market maker for three distinct risks, not one. Order-processing cost is the pure operational cost of handling the trade — exchange fees, technology, and the cost of running the business. Inventory risk is the risk of holding a position between trades: once the market maker buys from one client, they're exposed to the price moving against them before they can offload it to the next client. Adverse selection is the risk of trading against a counterparty who knows something the market maker doesn't — if informed traders are more likely to hit one side of the quote right before news breaks, the market maker systematically loses on those trades. All three get priced into the spread, which is why spreads widen in volatile or uncertain conditions (inventory and adverse-selection risk both rise) and narrow in calm, liquid markets.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as the market maker charging three separate insurance premiums bundled into one number. The processing cost is small and boring. Inventory risk is 'I might get stuck holding this.' Adverse selection is the scary one — it's the risk that the person trading against you knows more than you do, and it's exactly why spreads blow out right before news: everyone suddenly suspects the next order might be informed.
questions.example: In a calm, liquid large-cap stock, a one-cent spread might be almost entirely order-processing cost. Right before an earnings release on a smaller, thinly traded name, the same market maker might quote a spread ten times wider — not because their operational costs changed, but because inventory risk and adverse selection both just spiked.
commonMistakes: Describing the spread as pure profit with no underlying risk being compensated
Naming only one of the three components (usually just 'risk' in general) instead of all three
Confusing adverse selection with simple price volatility rather than information asymmetry
Assuming the spread is fixed rather than dynamically widening with uncertainty
keyPoints: Order-processing cost: the operational cost of handling the trade
Inventory risk: exposure to price moves while holding a position between trades
Adverse selection: the risk of trading against a better-informed counterparty
Spreads widen when inventory risk and adverse selection both rise (volatile, uncertain conditions)
The spread is a market maker's compensation mechanism, not an arbitrary fee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names all three spread components
Explains why each component represents real risk, not just cost
Connects spread width to volatility/uncertainty conditions

questions.title: Market Order or Limit Order?
questions.prompt: You need to exit a position right now because a risk limit was just breached. Another trader wants to buy 5,000 shares of a thinly traded stock but refuses to pay more than $20.10. Which order type does each situation call for, and what does each type guarantee — and not guarantee?
questions.modelAnswer: A market order guarantees execution but not price — it fills immediately against the best resting orders on the book, whatever that price happens to be. That's the right tool for someone who needs out right now because a risk limit was breached: certainty of getting flat matters more than the exact exit price. A limit order guarantees price but not execution — it only fills at the specified price or better, and if the market never reaches that price, it simply rests unfilled on the book. That's the right tool for the trader who has a hard price ceiling of $20.10 and would rather not trade at all than pay more.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame it to someone new: a market order says 'I don't care what price, just get me out,' and a limit order says 'I care about price more than I care about whether this fills at all.' The risk-limit breach is a market-order situation almost by definition — the whole point of a hard limit is that you act immediately, not that you wait for a better price.
questions.example: If the stock's best bid is $20.05 and the trader with the $20.10 ceiling places a limit buy at $20.10, the order rests on the book until someone is willing to sell at $20.10 or below — it might fill instantly, might take hours, or might never fill if the price keeps rising.
commonMistakes: Saying a market order guarantees a good price rather than just guaranteeing execution
Thinking a limit order will always eventually fill if you just wait long enough
Recommending a limit order for the risk-breach exit, missing that certainty of execution is the priority there
Confusing a limit order with a stop order
keyPoints: Market order: guarantees execution, not price
Limit order: guarantees price (or better), not execution
A forced, urgent exit calls for a market order
A hard price ceiling/floor with no urgency calls for a limit order
An unfilled limit order simply rests on the book

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches each scenario to the right order type
States what each order type guarantees and does not guarantee
Explains the reasoning (urgency vs. price control) behind the choice

questions.title: What a Market Maker Actually Does
questions.prompt: Explain what a market maker is and why they're willing to take the other side of trades all day. What's the real risk they're managing, and how do they get compensated for taking it on?
questions.modelAnswer: A market maker is a firm that continuously quotes both a bid and an ask for a security, standing ready to buy or sell at those prices. This provides liquidity — other participants can trade immediately instead of waiting for a natural counterparty to show up. The real risk the market maker manages is inventory risk: every time they fill one side of a trade, they end up holding a position they didn't necessarily want, exposed to the price moving against them before they can offload it. They're compensated through the bid-ask spread — buying at the bid and selling at the ask, pocketing the difference across many trades, which over time pays for the risk of holding that inventory and the risk of occasionally trading against better-informed counterparties.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a market maker as being in the business of being available, not the business of predicting direction. They don't care whether the stock goes up or down — they care about capturing the spread over and over, and managing the inventory that builds up as a side effect of always being willing to quote both sides.
questions.example: A market maker quotes 99.95 bid / 100.05 ask. A customer sells 1,000 shares into the bid, then a different customer buys 1,000 shares at the ask. The market maker bought at 99.95 and sold at 100.05 on the same shares, capturing (100.05 - 99.95) x 1,000 = $100 — with no directional view taken at all.
commonMistakes: Describing a market maker as someone trying to predict where the price is headed
Confusing a market maker (a dealer, trading from their own account) with a broker (an agent, just executing on a client's behalf)
Missing that the spread is compensation for inventory and information risk, not just a toll
Assuming a market maker always makes money on every single trade rather than on average across many
keyPoints: A market maker continuously quotes both a bid and an ask
They provide liquidity so other participants can trade immediately
The real risk is inventory risk — holding an unwanted position between trades
Compensation comes from capturing the bid-ask spread repeatedly, not from directional bets
A market maker is a dealer (principal), not a broker (agent)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a market maker's role and liquidity function
Identifies inventory risk as the core risk being managed
Explains the spread as the compensation mechanism

questions.title: Call Option Payoff and Breakeven
questions.prompt: You buy a call option with a strike of $40 for a premium of $3. At expiration, the stock is trading at $46. What's the payoff, what's your profit, and what stock price would you have needed just to break even?
questions.code:
Call payoff = max(S - K, 0)
Profit (buyer) = payoff - premium
Breakeven (long call) = K + premium
questions.modelAnswer: The payoff at expiration is max(S - K, 0) = max(46 - 40, 0) = $6. Profit is the payoff minus the premium paid: 6 - 3 = $3. Breakeven for a long call is strike plus premium: 40 + 3 = $43 — the stock needed to clear $43 just to recover the cost of the option before any real profit started. Everything above $43 at expiration is pure profit for the buyer; everything between $40 and $43 means the option finished in-the-money but still a net loss once the premium is accounted for.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap here is stopping at the payoff and calling that the answer. $6 of payoff isn't $6 of profit — you paid $3 for the right, so that comes out first. I always compute breakeven before anything else on a new position, because it's the number that actually tells you whether the trade was worth putting on.
questions.example: S=$46, K=$40, premium=$3. Payoff = max(46-40,0) = $6. Profit = 6 - 3 = $3. Breakeven = 40 + 3 = $43.
commonMistakes: Reporting the $6 payoff as the profit, forgetting to subtract the premium
Computing breakeven as just the strike, ignoring the premium paid
Mixing up the call payoff formula with the put formula (max(K-S,0))
Assuming any in-the-money option is automatically profitable
keyPoints: Call payoff = max(S - K, 0)
Profit for the buyer = payoff minus premium paid
Breakeven for a long call = strike + premium
An in-the-money option can still be a net loss once premium is subtracted

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Computes payoff correctly
Computes profit correctly (subtracting premium)
Computes breakeven correctly and explains what it means

questions.title: What Delta Actually Tells a Trader
questions.prompt: A trader tells you a call option has a delta of 0.65. What does that number actually mean in plain terms, and what range can delta take for calls versus puts?
questions.modelAnswer: Delta is the sensitivity of an option's value to a $1 move in the underlying stock — it's the partial derivative of the option's price with respect to the stock price. A delta of 0.65 means that for a $1 increase in the stock, the call's value is expected to rise by roughly $0.65, and for a $1 decrease, it's expected to fall by roughly $0.65. Call delta ranges from 0 to 1 — it rises toward 1 as the option moves deep in-the-money (where it starts behaving like owning the stock outright) and falls toward 0 deep out-of-the-money. Put delta ranges from -1 to 0, since puts gain value as the stock falls.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of delta as 'how many shares of stock does this option behave like, right now, for a small move.' A 0.65 delta call is behaving, in that instant, like holding 65 shares. It's not a fixed number though — it shifts constantly as the stock moves, which is exactly the gamma conversation that comes right after this one.
questions.example: A call with delta 0.65 on a stock at $100 that ticks up to $101 should gain roughly $0.65 in value, all else equal — a quick sanity check a trader can do mentally before even looking at a pricing model.
commonMistakes: Thinking delta is a fixed, permanent number rather than a sensitivity that changes as the stock moves
Giving put delta a range of 0 to 1 instead of -1 to 0
Confusing delta with the probability the option expires in-the-money (a related but distinct concept)
Forgetting that delta is specifically a per-$1-move sensitivity, not a percentage
keyPoints: Delta = sensitivity of option value to a $1 move in the underlying
Call delta ranges from 0 to 1
Put delta ranges from -1 to 0
Delta rises toward the extreme as an option moves deep in- or out-of-the-money
Delta is a snapshot, not a fixed constant

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what delta measures in plain terms
States the correct range for call delta and put delta
Notes that delta changes as the underlying moves

questions.title: What a VaR Number Actually Promises
questions.prompt: Your desk reports '1-day 99% VaR of $2 million.' A junior trader reads this as 'we can never lose more than $2 million in a day.' Correct that interpretation — what does the statement actually mean, and what two things always have to be specified for a VaR number to be meaningful at all?
questions.modelAnswer: A 1-day 99% VaR of $2 million means that on no more than 1% of trading days, the portfolio is expected to lose more than $2 million — it is explicitly not a statement that losses can never exceed that number. It means that outcome is supposed to be rare, specifically a roughly 1-in-100-day event, and on the worst days it absolutely can lose more than $2 million. Two things always have to be stated for a VaR number to mean anything: the confidence level (95%, 99%, etc.) and the horizon (1-day, 10-day, etc.) — 'VaR is $2 million' on its own, without both of those, is an incomplete statement.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of the most common misreadings on a desk, and it's worth correcting early because it leads to real overconfidence. VaR tells you where the common range of bad days ends, not where the worst case ends. The number says nothing at all about how bad the 1% of days beyond that threshold actually get — that's exactly the gap Expected Shortfall is built to fill.
questions.example: If a firm's 1-day 99% VaR is $2 million, over 100 trading days you'd expect roughly one day where the loss exceeds $2 million — and on that one day, the loss could be $2.1 million or $20 million; VaR alone doesn't distinguish between those two outcomes.
commonMistakes: Treating VaR as a hard ceiling or worst-case loss rather than a threshold that's occasionally exceeded
Quoting a VaR number without specifying the confidence level or horizon
Assuming a breach of VaR is itself evidence something is broken, rather than an expected, if rare, occurrence
Confusing VaR with the average loss in the tail (which is what Expected Shortfall measures)
keyPoints: VaR is a threshold not expected to be exceeded with a given confidence, not a hard cap
A breach is expected to happen occasionally — that's what the confidence level implies
Confidence level and horizon must both be specified
VaR says nothing about how severe a loss beyond the threshold could be

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Corrects the junior trader's misinterpretation accurately
Explains the correct probabilistic meaning of the VaR statement
Names both required components: confidence level and horizon

questions.title: Price-Time Priority, Explained to a New Hire
questions.prompt: Two resting buy orders sit at the same price on the limit order book. How does the exchange decide which one gets filled first when a matching sell order arrives? What happens to that priority if a trader cancels and re-submits their order at the same price?
questions.modelAnswer: The standard rule is price-time priority: among orders at the same price, the order that arrived first gets filled first. Better prices always have priority over worse prices regardless of timing, but once two orders are tied on price, time of arrival breaks the tie. Most exchanges reset an order's time priority whenever its price is changed — so canceling and re-submitting an order at the same price typically sends it to the back of the queue at that price level, because the system treats it as a brand-new order rather than preserving its original arrival time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The practical lesson here, especially for anyone tempted to constantly fiddle with a resting order, is that canceling and replacing isn't free — you lose your place in line. Price-time priority specifically rewards committing to a price early and discourages gaming the queue by canceling and resubmitting just to 'improve' your position without actually improving your price.
questions.example: If Trader A's buy order at $50.00 arrived at 9:31:05 and Trader B's buy order at $50.00 arrived at 9:31:07, an incoming sell order crossing $50.00 fills Trader A first. If Trader A then cancels and resubmits at $50.00 at 9:35:00, they lose their original time priority and now sit behind Trader B.
commonMistakes: Assuming orders at the same price are filled in some order other than time of arrival (e.g., randomly, or by size)
Thinking that canceling and resubmitting at the same price preserves the original queue position
Confusing price-time priority with the NBBO (a separate concept about the best price across venues)
Forgetting that a better price always beats a worse price regardless of timing
keyPoints: Better price always fills first, regardless of arrival time
Among orders at the same price, earliest arrival fills first
Most exchanges reset time priority when an order's price is changed
This discourages constantly canceling and replacing orders just to cut in line

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains price-time priority
Correctly explains what happens to priority on cancel/resubmit
Explains the practical/behavioral implication of this rule

questions.title: Monty Hall, Explained Under Interview Pressure
questions.prompt: Three doors, one car, two goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other two doors and always reveals a goat. Should you switch to the remaining door? Walk through why, without just citing the answer from memory.
questions.modelAnswer: Yes, you should switch — switching wins with probability 2/3, staying wins with probability 1/3. The key fact most people miss is that the host's reveal is not random: he is constrained to always open a goat door among the two you didn't pick, so his action carries information. Enumerate by your original pick: if you picked the car (probability 1/3), the host opens one of the two goat doors and switching loses. If you picked a goat (probability 2/3), the host is forced to open the other goat door, leaving the car behind the remaining door, so switching wins. Switching simply inherits the 2/3 probability that your first guess was wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trick that makes this click for most people is realizing the host isn't opening a random door — he's constrained. If you picked wrong, which happens two-thirds of the time, he has no choice but to reveal the only other goat, which means the car is sitting behind the door you'd switch to. I'd also mention that if I were unsure under interview pressure, a 30-second mental simulation — 'if I always switch, I win exactly when my first pick was a goat, which is 2/3 of the time' — is a legitimate way to double-check the answer live.
questions.example: Running this as a simulation: pick a door uniformly at random 400,000 times, and track whether 'always switch' wins. The simulated switch-win rate converges to almost exactly 2/3, matching the theoretical answer.
commonMistakes: Assuming the remaining two doors are now 50/50 because 'one goat was removed'
Treating the host's reveal as random information rather than constrained, informative information
Being unable to explain *why* the answer is 2/3, even if the memorized answer is correct
Confusing this with a simpler problem where no doors are deliberately revealed
keyPoints: Switching wins with probability 2/3; staying wins with probability 1/3
The host's reveal is constrained (always a goat), not random, which is the source of the information
Enumerating by the original pick (car vs. goat) is the clean way to derive the answer
Switching inherits the 2/3 probability that the first guess was wrong
A quick simulation is a legitimate way to verify the answer under pressure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives the correct answer (switch, 2/3 vs 1/3)
Correctly explains the host's constrained reveal as the key mechanism
Walks through the enumeration/derivation rather than just stating the answer

questions.title: Why Not Just Bet the Full Edge Every Time?
questions.prompt: You're offered a repeated, favorable bet: 60% chance to win even money. A junior trader argues the expected value is maximized by betting your entire bankroll every round, so that's what you should do. What's wrong with that reasoning?
questions.modelAnswer: Betting the entire bankroll every round does maximize expected value per round, but it also guarantees eventual ruin with probability 1 — a single loss wipes out the entire bankroll, and with a 40% chance of losing each round, that loss is only a matter of time. Expected value and survivability are different questions. The Kelly criterion instead asks what fraction of the bankroll, re-bet each round, maximizes the long-run growth rate of wealth — for this bet (p=0.6, even odds), that works out to f* = p - (1-p)/b = 0.6 - 0.4/1 = 0.20, or 20% of the bankroll per round, not 100%.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the single most important lesson in sizing: a positive expected value doesn't mean you should bet without limit. 'Maximize expected value per bet' and 'maximize how your wealth actually grows over many bets' are different objectives, and betting everything every time destroys the second one even while technically satisfying the first. I'd want the junior trader to internalize that before they ever size a real position.
questions.example: Simulating repeated log-growth at different bet fractions on this exact bet shows growth peaking around f=0.20 (the Kelly fraction) and turning negative by f=0.40 — double the Kelly size — even though every single bet in the sequence still has positive expected value.
commonMistakes: Equating 'maximizes expected value' with 'is the correct bet size'
Not recognizing that betting 100% of a bankroll on a repeated bet leads to ruin with certainty
Being unable to state or apply the Kelly formula f* = p - (1-p)/b
Assuming any positive-EV bet can be sized arbitrarily large without consequence
keyPoints: Maximizing expected value per bet is not the same as maximizing long-run growth
Betting the entire bankroll on a repeated favorable bet still leads to ruin with probability 1
Kelly fraction f* = p - (1-p)/b maximizes long-run log-growth of wealth
For p=0.6, b=1: f* = 0.20 — bet 20% of the bankroll, not 100%
Overbetting a genuinely positive-EV bet can still produce negative long-run growth

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the flaw in 'maximize EV means bet everything'
Explains that full-bankroll betting leads to eventual ruin
References the Kelly criterion and computes or cites the correct fraction

questions.title: Slippage vs. Market Impact
questions.prompt: Two traders both complain their fill was worse than expected. One blames 'the market moving on me.' The other blames 'my own order being too big.' Which complaint describes slippage, and which describes market impact — and why does the distinction actually matter?
questions.modelAnswer: The first trader is describing slippage — the difference between the price expected when the decision to trade was made and the price actually achieved, driven by the market moving between decision and execution, independent of the trader's own order size. The second trader is describing market impact — the cost caused by the trader's own order being large enough that it has to walk through multiple price levels on the book to get filled, pushing the price against itself. The distinction matters because the fixes are different: slippage is reduced by trading faster or at calmer times, while market impact is reduced by breaking a large order into smaller pieces over time (e.g., using VWAP or TWAP) — a slippage problem doesn't go away by slicing an order, and a market-impact problem doesn't go away by trading faster.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell both traders: one of you is being hit by something outside your control, the other is partly hitting yourself. Slippage is the market doing something to you; market impact is what your own size does to the market. Getting that distinction right matters because you'd reach for completely different tools to fix each one.
questions.example: A small order that fills instantly at the quoted price but the quote had already moved since the decision was made — that's slippage. A large order that eats through five price levels on the book, each one worse than the last, as it fills — that's market impact, and it happens even if the quoted price never moved before the order arrived.
commonMistakes: Treating slippage and market impact as the same thing
Assuming both are fixed the same way (e.g., 'just trade faster' for both)
Missing that market impact scales with the trader's own order size relative to available liquidity
Attributing a large order's bad fill entirely to 'the market,' ignoring the trader's own footprint
keyPoints: Slippage: the market moving between decision and fill, independent of the trader's size
Market impact: the cost caused by the trader's own order size moving the price
Slippage is reduced by timing; market impact is reduced by slicing the order
Confusing the two leads to applying the wrong fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies which trader describes slippage vs. market impact
Explains the causal difference between the two
Explains why the distinction changes what fix is appropriate

questions.title: Quick EV: Should You Take the Bet?
questions.prompt: Someone offers you this bet: flip a fair coin. Heads, you win $150. Tails, you lose $100. Out loud, in under 15 seconds: what's the expected value, and would you take the bet?
questions.modelAnswer: EV = 0.5 x 150 + 0.5 x (-100) = 75 - 50 = $25. The expected value is positive, so on a per-trial basis this is a favorable bet. Whether to actually take it depends on more than just the sign of EV — bet size relative to bankroll, how many times you can repeat it, and variance tolerance all matter — but as a standalone 'is this favorable' question, yes, take it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Half of 150 is 75, half of 100 is 50, 75 minus 50 is 25 — that's the whole calculation, and it should take seconds, not a notepad. The instinct to immediately flag 'positive EV doesn't automatically mean bet your whole stack' is exactly the right follow-up thought, even though this question is really just testing the arithmetic speed.
questions.example: EV = 0.5(150) + 0.5(-100) = 75 - 50 = $25 per flip, on average, if repeated many times.
commonMistakes: Averaging the two outcomes incorrectly (e.g., just taking (150-100)/2 without weighting by probability, which happens to work here only because probabilities are equal — doing it correctly as a weighted sum matters for non-50/50 bets)
Taking too long or reaching for a calculator for genuinely simple arithmetic
Forgetting to account for the negative sign on the loss outcome
Conflating 'positive EV' with 'you should always take any size of this bet'
keyPoints: EV = sum of (probability x outcome) across all outcomes
Positive EV means favorable on average over many repetitions
Speed and accuracy under light pressure is the actual skill being tested here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Computes the correct EV ($25)
States clearly that positive EV makes the bet favorable
Does the calculation quickly without unnecessary steps

questions.title: Quick P&L: Short Position Drill
questions.prompt: You're short 800 shares at $45. The stock drops to $41.75. What's your P&L? Answer immediately, then explain the sign logic for a second.
questions.modelAnswer: P&L = (45 - 41.75) x 800 = 3.25 x 800 = $2,600 profit. A short position gains when the price falls, so the correct direction for the arithmetic is entry price minus exit price (not exit minus entry), multiplied by shares. Getting the sign right instantly — rather than computing the magnitude and then guessing whether it's a gain or a loss — is the actual skill drilled here.
questions.professionalAnswer: 3.25 times 800 — I'd break that into 3 x 800 = 2,400 plus 0.25 x 800 = 200, giving 2,600, all in my head in a couple of seconds. The sign check is automatic for a short: price went down, I'm short, that's a win, full stop — no hesitation on direction.
questions.example: Entry (short) at $45, exit (buy to cover) at $41.75, 800 shares: (45 - 41.75) x 800 = $2,600 profit.
commonMistakes: Computing exit minus entry instead of entry minus entry for a short position, flipping the sign
Taking too long on straightforward multiplication instead of breaking it into easy pieces
Second-guessing whether a falling price is good or bad for a short position
Forgetting to multiply by share count after getting the per-share P&L right
keyPoints: Short P&L = (entry price - exit price) x shares
A falling price is a gain for a short position
Breaking multiplication into round pieces speeds up mental math
The sign should be obvious before the arithmetic even starts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Computes the correct P&L ($2,600 profit)
Gets the sign/direction correct without hesitation
Explains the short-position sign logic clearly

questions.title: Mental Math: 19 x 21 in Your Head
questions.prompt: Multiply 19 x 21 without a calculator, in under 5 seconds, and explain the trick you used.
questions.modelAnswer: 19 and 21 are both 1 away from the midpoint 20, so write them as (20-1)(20+1) = 20^2 - 1^2 = 400 - 1 = 399. This is the difference-of-squares trick: for two numbers equidistant from a convenient round midpoint m with half-difference d, the product is m^2 - d^2, which turns an awkward two-digit multiplication into squaring a round number and subtracting a small square.
questions.professionalAnswer: The second I see two numbers that are close together and straddle a round number, I'm not multiplying them directly — I'm squaring the midpoint and subtracting the square of the gap. 20 squared is 400, the gap is 1, 1 squared is 1, so 399. That's genuinely faster than long multiplication once the pattern is automatic.
questions.example: 17 x 23 works the same way: midpoint 20, half-difference 3, so 20^2 - 3^2 = 400 - 9 = 391.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to standard long multiplication instead of recognizing the equidistant-from-midpoint pattern
Picking the wrong midpoint or miscomputing the half-difference
Forgetting to square the half-difference (using d instead of d^2)
Taking noticeably longer than the few seconds this trick should require
keyPoints: (m-d)(m+d) = m^2 - d^2 for numbers equidistant from midpoint m
19 x 21: midpoint 20, half-difference 1, so 400 - 1 = 399
Squaring a round number and a small number is much faster than two-digit multiplication
Works whenever two numbers straddle a convenient midpoint

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives the correct answer (399) quickly
Correctly explains the difference-of-squares trick
Demonstrates the general pattern, not just a memorized answer

questions.title: Quick Breakeven Drill: Long Put
questions.prompt: You buy a put with strike $60 for a premium of $2.50. What stock price is the exact breakeven at expiration? Answer in under 10 seconds.
questions.modelAnswer: Breakeven for a long put is strike minus premium: 60 - 2.50 = $57.50. Below $57.50 at expiration, the position is profitable; between $57.50 and $60 it's in-the-money but still a net loss once the premium is accounted for; above $60 the put expires worthless and the full premium is lost.
questions.professionalAnswer: Put breakeven is strike minus premium, mirror image of a call's strike-plus-premium — I don't even think about it as a formula anymore, it's just automatic. 60 minus 2.50 is 57.50, done.
commonMistakes: Adding the premium instead of subtracting it (using the call formula for a put)
Reporting the strike itself as the breakeven, ignoring the premium
Confusing breakeven with the point where the option first has intrinsic value (which is just the strike)
Taking longer than a couple of seconds on simple subtraction
keyPoints: Breakeven for a long put = strike - premium
Below breakeven: profitable; above the strike: full premium lost
This is the mirror image of the long-call breakeven formula (strike + premium)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives the correct breakeven ($57.50)
States the correct formula direction (subtract, not add)

questions.title: Quick Delta-Hedge Share Count
questions.prompt: A dealer just sold 20 call option contracts (each covering 100 shares), and each option has a delta of 0.40. How many shares should the dealer buy to delta-hedge the position, and in which direction?
questions.modelAnswer: Total delta exposure from the short calls = 20 contracts x 100 shares x 0.40 delta = 800 delta-shares. Since the dealer is short the calls, they're short delta and need to buy stock to neutralize it: buy 800 shares. That brings the combined position (short calls plus long 800 shares) to approximately zero net delta for small moves in the stock.
questions.professionalAnswer: 20 contracts times 100 shares is 2,000 shares of notional, times 0.40 delta is 800 — that's the whole calculation, done in one line. Short the calls means short delta, so the hedge direction is to buy stock, not sell it.
questions.example: 20 x 100 x 0.40 = 800 shares to buy, to offset being short delta from the written calls.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the 100-share contract multiplier
Hedging in the wrong direction (selling instead of buying against a short-call position)
Treating delta as a fixed hedge that never needs to be revisited (ignoring gamma)
Using the wrong sign because of confusion about long vs. short option positions
keyPoints: Delta-hedge shares = contracts x contract multiplier x delta
Short calls = short delta, hedged by buying stock

questions.title: Quick Counting: Splitting Risk Across Desks
questions.prompt: A desk has 6 identical units of risk budget to allocate across 3 strategies, any split allowed including zero. Without listing them all out, how many distinct ways can this be done?

questions.title: Quick Kelly Sizing Drill
questions.prompt: A bet wins with probability 0.55 and pays even money (b=1). What fraction of the bankroll does the Kelly criterion say to bet? Compute it immediately.

questions.professionalAnswer: Spread times size — 20 cents times 2,000 shares is $400. The key phrase in the question is 'no price move in between,' because that's exactly what makes this pure spread capture rather than a result that also depends on which way the stock happened to move.

questions.prompt: A portfolio has an expected daily return of 0.0% and a daily volatility of 1.5%. Using the parametric method and a z-score of 1.65 for 95% confidence, what's the 1-day 95% VaR, in percentage terms?

questions.title: Diagnosing a Growing One-Sided Inventory
questions.prompt: You're quoting both sides of a stock, and over the last hour you've noticed your position has quietly grown to a large net long — far more buy orders have hit your bid than sellers have hit your ask. What's actually happening, and what are your options for managing it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is inventory risk building up exactly as the mechanism predicts: more flow is hitting one side of the quote than the other, and each fill on the bid adds to a growing long position the quoter didn't necessarily want. There are a few standard levers: widen or skew the quote to make buying less attractive and selling more attractive (discouraging further one-sided flow while still being willing to trade), reduce size offered on the side that keeps getting hit, or actively offload part of the inventory in the open market rather than waiting for natural two-sided flow to balance it out. Letting it continue to build without any of these actions means growing directional exposure that was never actually intended.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer here is that I know this problem exists and I know the standard playbook — skew the quote, cut size, or hit the market directly to offload — but the actual live mechanics of exactly how much to skew a quote in real time, in response to real-time inventory, is a deeper market-making engineering problem than this course's foundational market-structure lessons go into. I'd want to be upfront that I'm reasoning from general industry knowledge of what a market maker does, not from a specific lesson that walks through the live quoting algorithm itself.
questions.example: A quoter who started the day flat and is now long 50,000 shares after an hour of one-sided buying flow has three honest choices: skew quotes to discourage more buying, cut the size shown on the bid, or actively sell some of the inventory into the market to flatten back toward neutral.

Doing nothing leaves unintended directional exposure growing unchecked

questions.title: Why Your Delta Hedge Drifted Out of Balance
questions.prompt: This morning you delta-hedged a long call position perfectly — combined delta was zero. By afternoon, after the stock moved several dollars, your position has meaningful net delta exposure again, even though you didn't trade anything. What happened, and what should you do?
questions.modelAnswer: Delta is only accurate for a small, instantaneous move — as the stock actually moves meaningfully, delta itself changes, and that rate of change is exactly what gamma measures. A hedge that was perfectly neutral at one stock price is no longer neutral once the stock has moved several dollars, because the option's delta has shifted even though the stock hedge (the fixed number of shares held) hasn't. The fix is to rebalance: recompute the option's current delta at the new stock price and adjust the stock position to match, which is a repeated, ongoing task for any position with meaningful gamma, not a one-time setup.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'gamma is the reason you have to keep retrading your hedge' lesson. Nothing is broken — this is expected behavior for any option position, and it's exactly why a desk with a lot of gamma exposure rebalances frequently rather than setting a hedge once and walking away.
questions.example: A call with delta 0.50 hedged with -50 shares per contract is neutral at the stock's current price. If the stock rallies and the call's delta rises to 0.70, the position is now under-hedged by 20 delta-shares per contract and needs 20 more shares sold short per contract to restore neutrality.
commonMistakes: Assuming a delta hedge, once set, stays correct indefinitely
Not recognizing gamma as the specific mechanism causing the drift
Treating the drifted exposure as a sign of a broken position rather than an expected consequence of holding options
Failing to propose rebalancing as the concrete next action
keyPoints: Delta is only accurate for small, instantaneous moves
Gamma measures how fast delta itself changes as the underlying moves
A hedge that was neutral at one price is not automatically neutral at a new price
The fix is to recompute delta and rebalance the stock hedge, repeatedly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies gamma as the cause of the drift

questions.title: A Backtest Looked Great, Live Trading Lost Money
questions.prompt: A strategy showed a Sharpe ratio of 2.5 in its backtest. Deployed live, it has lost money steadily for three months. Before assuming the market simply changed, what two data-related problems in the original backtest would you want to rule out first?
questions.modelAnswer: The two classic culprits that make a backtest look better than reality are look-ahead bias and survivorship bias. Look-ahead bias means the backtest's simulated decisions used information that wouldn't actually have been available at that point in time — a missing shift on a signal, parameters tuned on the full dataset, or restated data applied retroactively. Survivorship bias means the backtest's universe was built from instruments that still exist today, silently excluding everything that went bankrupt or was delisted, which inflates the measured historical return of nearly any strategy trading that universe. A Sharpe of 2.5 is itself unusually high and should have prompted a re-check for exactly these two issues before the strategy was ever deployed, not just afterward.
questions.professionalAnswer: A Sharpe above 2 is the kind of number that should make you suspicious of your own process before you get excited about it. My first move wouldn't be to blame the market — it'd be to go back and check whether the backtest's signal construction had a lookahead leak, and whether the universe used point-in-time membership or today's survivors applied retroactively to history.
questions.example: A backtest that builds its universe from 'today's S&P 500 constituents' and tests back to 2010 silently excludes every constituent that was removed since then for underperforming or going bankrupt — inflating the apparent historical return of any strategy trading that universe, including a simple buy-and-hold.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to 'the market regime changed' without first auditing the backtest itself
Not recognizing an unusually high Sharpe ratio as a red flag worth investigating
Checking for only one of the two biases instead of both
Assuming the live underperformance alone proves the strategy's underlying idea was wrong
keyPoints: Look-ahead bias: using information that wasn't actually available at the simulated decision point
Survivorship bias: building the universe from today's survivors, excluding historical failures
Both biases make a backtest look better than reality, in the same direction
An unusually high Sharpe ratio (like 2.5) should itself trigger a re-check for these issues

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names look-ahead bias and survivorship bias

questions.title: Recognizing When a Kill Switch Should Fire
questions.prompt: A live strategy has a pre-set daily loss limit of -$10,000 and a max drawdown limit of -$15,000. Today it's down $11,200 on the day, with the drawdown at -$9,000. What should happen, automatically, and why is it important that this isn't a judgment call made in the moment?
questions.modelAnswer: The daily loss limit of -$10,000 has been breached (the strategy is down $11,200), so the kill switch should trigger automatically: stop placing new orders and, typically, flatten existing positions. The drawdown limit hasn't been breached (-$9,000 is still within the -$15,000 limit), but it doesn't need to be — any one of the pre-committed hard limits being crossed is enough to trigger. The entire point of setting these as hard numbers in advance is that nobody has to make a judgment call in the heat of a bad day; the system already decided what 'too much' means before the bad day arrived, removing the human hesitation that tends to make losses worse in a real crisis.
questions.professionalAnswer: This should be boring and automatic — the daily loss limit was crossed, so trading stops, full stop, no discussion. The value of a kill switch isn't in the threshold number itself, it's in removing the moment where someone might think 'just a little more time, it'll come back.'
questions.example: Even though the drawdown limit (-$15,000) hasn't been hit, the daily loss limit (-$10,000) was breached at -$11,200 — either limit alone is sufficient to trigger the kill switch; they aren't both required.
commonMistakes: Thinking both limits need to be breached simultaneously before the kill switch fires
Suggesting a human should 'wait and see' before pulling the trigger on a breached hard limit
Missing that the daily loss limit was already crossed in this scenario
Not explaining why pre-committing the limit in advance matters (removing in-the-moment hesitation)
keyPoints: Any single pre-committed hard limit being breached should trigger the kill switch
The daily loss limit was breached here (-$11,200 vs. -$10,000 limit)
The drawdown limit was not breached, but that's irrelevant once another limit is crossed
Setting the limit in advance removes human hesitation in the moment of a real loss

questions.title: A Network Hiccup Nearly Doubled a Position
questions.prompt: An order submission timed out, so the system retried it automatically. It turns out the original order had actually gone through — the retry risked creating a second, duplicate position. What design pattern prevents this, and why is it non-negotiable rather than a nice-to-have?
questions.modelAnswer: The standard defense is a client order ID: a unique identifier the submitting system generates and attaches to every order, which the broker treats as a de-duplication key. Retrying a submission with the same client order ID must not create a second order — the broker (or the internal order management system) recognizes the ID and either returns the existing order's status or simply does nothing further, rather than placing a duplicate. This is non-negotiable because a dropped network response during a routine retry is a completely ordinary, frequent occurrence in live trading — not a rare edge case — and without this pattern, it's a real, common cause of accidentally doubling a position, almost never a problem that would ever show up in a backtest.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is exactly the kind of problem that never appears until you're trading real size with real money, because a backtest never has a network at all. Idempotent submission via a client order ID isn't a nice engineering touch — it's the difference between a dropped acknowledgment being a non-event and it being an accidental double position that someone has to explain later.
questions.example: If client order ID 'algo-2024-001' is submitted, acknowledged, but the acknowledgment is lost in transit, resubmitting with the exact same ID should return the already-placed order rather than creating a second 1,000-share position alongside the first.
commonMistakes: Proposing to simply retry without any de-duplication mechanism
Treating this as a rare edge case rather than a routine, expected failure mode
Not naming the client order ID / idempotent submission pattern specifically
Assuming this kind of bug would show up in a backtest, when it's specific to live execution infrastructure
keyPoints: A client order ID is a unique de-duplication key attached to every order submission
Idempotent submission: resubmitting the same ID has no additional effect beyond the first success
Network failures during order submission are routine, not rare, in live trading
Without this pattern, a dropped acknowledgment can silently double a position

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies idempotent submission via a client order ID as the fix
Explains why this failure mode is routine rather than rare in live trading

questions.title: Why Did the Spread Suddenly Triple?
questions.prompt: A stock that normally trades with a one-cent spread suddenly shows a three-cent spread an hour before an earnings announcement, with no change in the company's actual business. Is this a market malfunction, and what's driving it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a malfunction — it's the spread doing exactly what it's supposed to do. Two of the three components that make up the spread rise sharply right before an earnings announcement: inventory risk rises because the price is about to become much more uncertain, making it riskier to hold a position between trades, and adverse selection risk rises because anyone trading right before the announcement is more likely to have an informational edge. Order-processing cost stays roughly flat. Widening the spread is the market maker's rational response to both of those risks spiking simultaneously, not a sign that anything is broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell someone worried about this: nothing is malfunctioning, the market is pricing in exactly the right amount of extra caution. Right before a known information event, both inventory risk and adverse selection spike at the same time, and a wider spread is the market maker's normal, rational way of getting paid more for taking on more risk in that specific window.
questions.example: The same stock's spread typically narrows back down within minutes of the earnings release actually being public, once the uncertainty that drove the widening has resolved.
commonMistakes: Interpreting the wider spread as a sign of a broken or malfunctioning market
Attributing the widening only to 'volatility' in a vague sense rather than naming the specific mechanisms (inventory risk and adverse selection)
Missing that order-processing cost is the one component that does not meaningfully change here
Assuming the spread will stay wide indefinitely rather than normalizing once the event passes
keyPoints: Spread widening before a known event is rational, not a malfunction
Inventory risk rises because the near-term price outcome is uncertain
Adverse selection risk rises because pre-announcement traders are more likely informed
The spread typically narrows again once the uncertainty resolves

questions.title: Why Your Pairs Trade Stopped Converging
questions.prompt: You've been trading a pairs strategy on two historically highly correlated stocks for months. Recently the spread between them has drifted wider and wider without converging back, and your position keeps losing money. What's the most likely underlying problem?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely problem is that the pair was correlated but never truly cointegrated — correlation alone doesn't guarantee the spread between two instruments is mean-reverting, and two prices can be highly correlated over a sample while still wandering apart permanently. A pairs trade only makes real sense when there's a stable, mean-reverting long-run relationship (cointegration), tested properly rather than assumed from a high correlation number. A spread that keeps drifting without converging is a direct symptom of exactly this: either the relationship was never truly cointegrated, or a real structural change (a merger, a regulatory shift, one company's business diverging from the other's) has permanently broken a relationship that was once genuine.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the single most common mistake in pairs trading: confusing 'these two moved together in my sample' with 'these two have a genuine mean-reverting relationship.' A spread that just keeps widening instead of reverting is telling you, directly, that the assumption underneath the trade was wrong — either it was never really cointegrated, or something structural changed the relationship.
questions.example: Two stocks that both trended up together during a multi-year bull market can show high correlation in a backtest without ever being cointegrated — their prices happened to move in the same direction for reasons unrelated to each other, with no force actually pulling the spread back to a stable mean.

Treating a widening spread purely as 'bad luck' rather than evidence against the trade's core assumption
Confusing cointegration (a stable, mean-reverting long-run relationship) with simple correlation

A pairs trade needs a genuinely mean-reverting relationship, not just co-movement
A persistently widening, non-converging spread is a direct symptom of a correlation-only relationship or a structural break
Cointegration should be tested explicitly, not assumed from correlation

questions.title: Costless Backtest, Expensive Reality
questions.prompt: A daily-rebalancing strategy backtested with zero transaction costs showed a strong edge. Once real commissions and bid-ask spread costs are included, the edge almost completely disappears. Why would a daily-rebalancing strategy in particular be hit this hard, compared to one that trades monthly?
questions.modelAnswer: Transaction costs are charged on position changes, not on how much capital is managed — a strategy that rebalances its entire position every day pays the round-trip cost roughly 252 times a year, while one that rebalances monthly pays it only about 12 times. If each round-trip costs even a modest amount in basis points, that difference compounds into a dramatically larger annual cost drag for the daily strategy — easily large enough to turn an apparently profitable daily strategy into a loser once costs are included, even when the underlying signal is identical to the monthly version.
questions.professionalAnswer: Turnover is the variable that makes this obvious once you say it out loud: costs don't care about your edge, they care about how often you trade. A strategy that trades 20x more often than another one pays roughly 20x more in round-trip costs for the exact same signal, which is why 'ignore costs, the edge is there' is one of the most dangerous habits in early-stage backtesting.
questions.example: At 10 bps round-trip cost, a daily-rebalancing strategy pays roughly 252 x 0.10% ≈ 25% annual cost drag, while a monthly strategy pays roughly 12 x 0.10% ≈ 1.2% — a difference large enough to flip the daily strategy's net result from profitable to unprofitable even with an identical underlying signal.
commonMistakes: Assuming transaction costs scale with capital managed rather than with trading frequency
Not connecting the daily-vs-monthly difference specifically to turnover
Treating the cost erosion as evidence the signal itself was fake, rather than a frictions problem
Underestimating how much a seemingly small per-trade cost compounds at high frequency
keyPoints: Transaction costs are charged on position changes, not on assets under management
Daily rebalancing pays the round-trip cost roughly 252 times a year; monthly pays it about 12 times
High turnover amplifies even modest per-trade costs into large annual drag

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that costs scale with turnover, not capital

questions.title: How Leverage Turned a Normal Drawdown Into a Margin Call
questions.prompt: A strategy had an unlevered historical drawdown of about 20%. Running it at 2x leverage, a trader was forced out of the position by a margin call during a drawdown that, unlevered, wouldn't have been unusual at all. What went wrong, and was the strategy's edge actually broken?
questions.modelAnswer: Nothing about the underlying strategy's edge was necessarily broken — leverage doesn't change the Sharpe ratio, since it scales both return and volatility by the same factor, but it directly scales the dollar magnitude of drawdowns. A -20% unlevered drawdown becomes roughly -40% at 2x leverage, which is a dramatically more dangerous number relative to the capital actually posted as collateral. The real failure here was sizing: leverage can be forcibly reduced by a margin call at the worst possible time, locking in losses right before (or during) a drawdown that the unlevered version of the same strategy would have simply ridden through.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a sizing failure, not a signal failure — I'd be careful not to conclude the strategy is broken just because the levered account got margin-called. A -20% move becoming a -40% move at 2x leverage is just arithmetic; the real lesson is that leverage should be sized with the worst historical drawdown explicitly in mind, not applied on top of a number that was never meant to be levered that aggressively.
questions.example: A strategy with a historical -20% max drawdown, run at 2x leverage, should be expected to see roughly -40% drawdowns — a trader who sizes the levered account as if -20% were still the worst case is setting themselves up for exactly this kind of forced exit.

questions.title: Live Volatility Running Nearly Double the Backtest
questions.prompt: A strategy's backtest predicted daily P&L volatility of around $850. After a month live, the realized daily volatility is closer to $1,550 — a ratio of about 1.8x. Is this necessarily a sign the strategy is broken, and what should happen next?
questions.modelAnswer: A realized-to-expected volatility ratio of 1.8x is exactly the kind of signal that should trigger a review, but it doesn't automatically mean the strategy is broken — a single unusual bad day in a short live sample can move this ratio substantially on its own, which is a reminder of how much noise a short sample carries. The right response isn't to panic or immediately shut the strategy down, and it also isn't to ignore it; it's to review what's driving the gap (one anomalous day versus a genuine, sustained shift in behavior) and keep watching whether the elevated ratio persists over the following weeks. A sustained, growing gap over an extended period is a real signal; a short-sample spike driven by one event is not conclusive either way.
questions.professionalAnswer: A single month with one bad day can easily produce a ratio like this without the strategy being broken at all — I wouldn't treat this number in isolation as a verdict. The right move is to dig into what actually drove it, then keep watching: if it's still elevated after a few more weeks with no single obvious cause, that's a real warning sign worth escalating, not noise.
questions.example: If one injected bad day accounts for most of the volatility gap in an otherwise-normal month, the ratio could fall back toward 1.0 on its own over the following weeks without anything being fixed — which is exactly why a single month's ratio shouldn't be treated as a final verdict.

Failing to connect this to the broader theme of short-sample statistical noise

questions.title: What the Limit Order Book Has to Track
questions.prompt: At a basic level, what does a limit order book actually need to keep track of to function? Describe its structure in your own words.
questions.modelAnswer: The limit order book is the running list of all unfilled limit orders for a given security, organized into two sides: the bid side (resting buy orders, ranked from highest price down) and the ask side (resting sell orders, ranked from lowest price up). For each price level, the book needs to track the total resting quantity and, for correct matching, the arrival order of orders at that same price level (since price-time priority determines fill order among ties). The highest bid and lowest ask define the best bid and best ask, and the gap between them is the spread.
questions.professionalAnswer: At minimum, it's two ranked lists — one of buyers, one of sellers — each ordered by price, with ties broken by arrival time. Everything else (depth, NBBO across venues, spread) is just a derived view on top of that same underlying structure.
questions.example: A simplified book might show: bids at $50.02 (400 shares), $50.01 (900 shares); asks at $50.05 (300 shares), $50.07 (600 shares) — best bid $50.02, best ask $50.05, spread $0.03.
commonMistakes: Describing the book as a single unordered list rather than two ranked sides
Forgetting that ties at the same price need an arrival-time tiebreaker
Omitting quantity/depth at each price level, describing only the best price
Confusing the order book itself with the NBBO (which aggregates the best prices across multiple venues)
keyPoints: Two sides: bid (ranked high to low) and ask (ranked low to high)
Each price level tracks resting quantity
Ties at the same price are broken by arrival time (price-time priority)
Best bid and best ask define the spread

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the two-sided, price-ranked structure
Mentions quantity/depth tracking at each price level
Mentions the time-priority tiebreaker for orders at the same price
