questions.title: The States an Order Actually Moves Through
questions.prompt: Describe the lifecycle of an order from the moment it's submitted to a broker. What states can it move through, and why is 'is it filled, yes or no' an incomplete way to track it?
questions.modelAnswer: An order typically moves through NEW, then WORKING (acknowledged by the broker), then zero or more PARTIALLY_FILLED states, then FILLED — or it can be REJECTED outright (bad symbol, insufficient buying power, a risk check failure at the broker) or CANCELLED mid-way. Tracking only a binary 'filled or not' misses partial fills entirely — an order that's 40% filled is in a materially different, and important, state from one that's fully filled or one that was rejected before ever reaching the market, and a system that can't distinguish these will mishandle risk and position tracking.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd map it as: new, acknowledged, maybe several partial fills, then a final terminal state of filled, rejected, or cancelled. The partial-fill states are the ones people forget about when they design something quickly, and they happen constantly in real trading — far more often than a clean, single, all-at-once fill does for anything beyond a small order in a liquid name.
questions.example: A 1,000-share order might acknowledge, then receive three separate partial fills of 400, 350, and 250 shares at slightly different prices before reaching the terminal FILLED state with a blended average price.
commonMistakes: Treating order status as simply binary (filled or not filled)
Forgetting that an order can be rejected before it ever reaches the market
Not accounting for partial fills as their own meaningful intermediate state
Confusing cancellation (trader-initiated) with rejection (broker/exchange-initiated)
keyPoints: Lifecycle: NEW -> WORKING (acknowledged) -> PARTIALLY_FILLED (zero or more times) -> FILLED
Alternative terminal states: REJECTED or CANCELLED
A binary filled/not-filled view misses partial fills
Correct tracking of every state matters for accurate position and risk accounting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the main lifecycle states
Explains why partial fills matter and are commonly overlooked
Distinguishes rejection from cancellation

questions.title: Why Risk Limits Have to Be Code, Not a Spreadsheet
questions.prompt: A risk manager suggests that checking the daily loss limit once at the end of each trading day, in a spreadsheet, is good enough. Why is that insufficient for a live automated strategy, and what should replace it?
questions.modelAnswer: A once-a-day, manual spreadsheet check means the loss limit could be breached and continue to be breached for hours before anyone notices — by the time a human checks the spreadsheet at end of day, a strategy could have lost far more than the intended limit, with no automatic action taken in between. Live monitoring needs the same risk measures running continuously, evaluated after every trade or every market update, with the system able to act immediately the moment a limit is crossed. This requires risk checks and loss limits to be code that runs on every single update, not a formula someone checks when they remember to — that shift from a periodic human review to a continuous automated check is the entire engineering difference between a backtest report and a live kill switch.
questions.professionalAnswer: End-of-day spreadsheet checks are fine for a report, but they're not a risk control — a risk control has to be able to act in the moment the limit is breached, not hours later. The whole value of a kill switch is that it's evaluated continuously and acts automatically, which a spreadsheet simply cannot do.
questions.example: A strategy that breaches its daily loss limit at 10am but isn't checked until a 5pm spreadsheet review could continue trading and losing money for seven more hours with no automatic intervention at all.
commonMistakes: Agreeing that an end-of-day check is sufficient for a live, automated strategy
Not identifying the core problem as the delay between a breach and any action being taken
Proposing only a faster manual check rather than an automated, continuously-running one
Missing that this is specifically about automated strategies, where no human is watching in real time by default
keyPoints: A periodic manual check allows a breach to go unaddressed for hours
Risk checks need to run continuously, after every trade or update, not on a daily cadence
The fix is making risk limits automated code checks, not a spreadsheet formula
This continuous automation is what turns a risk measure into an actual kill switch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a once-daily check is insufficient
Proposes continuous, automated risk checking as the fix
Connects this to the concept of an automatic kill switch

questions.title: What a Clearinghouse Actually Does
questions.prompt: Explain what a clearinghouse (CCP) does once a trade is agreed, and why that process — called novation — is a major reason exchange-traded markets are considered safe to trade on, even between two complete strangers.
questions.modelAnswer: Once two parties agree to a trade, a central counterparty (CCP), or clearinghouse, inserts itself between the original buyer and seller immediately after the trade is agreed — a process called novation. The CCP becomes the seller to the original buyer and the buyer to the original seller, so each party now faces the CCP's credit risk instead of each other's. This matters because it means a trader never has to assess the creditworthiness of their actual counterparty on every single trade — they only have to trust the CCP, which is a far more concentrated, closely regulated, and typically well-capitalized risk — making it safe to trade anonymously with a complete stranger on an exchange.
questions.professionalAnswer: Novation is the mechanism that lets you trade with someone whose name you'll never know and whose creditworthiness you've never checked. The clearinghouse steps in and becomes the counterparty to both sides, so your actual exposure is to one well-capitalized, regulated entity instead of to whoever happened to be on the other side of your order.
questions.example: If Trader A buys from Trader B on an exchange, after novation Trader A's actual counterparty is the CCP (not Trader B), and the CCP's actual counterparty is Trader B — if Trader B later defaults, the CCP absorbs that risk rather than it passing through to Trader A.
commonMistakes: Describing the clearinghouse as merely a record-keeper rather than an actual risk-absorbing counterparty
Not naming novation specifically as the mechanism
Missing that this is what allows anonymous trading between strangers on an exchange
Confusing the clearinghouse's role with a broker's role
keyPoints: A CCP inserts itself between buyer and seller immediately after a trade is agreed
Novation: the CCP becomes seller to the buyer and buyer to the seller
Each party now faces the CCP's credit risk instead of the original counterparty's
This is what makes anonymous exchange trading between strangers safe

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the novation mechanism
Explains why this replaces counterparty-specific credit risk with CCP credit risk
Connects this to why anonymous exchange trading is considered safe

questions.title: TWAP and VWAP: The Basic Idea
questions.prompt: A desk needs to buy a large block of stock without moving the price too much against itself. Explain, structurally, how a TWAP algorithm and a VWAP algorithm each break up that order differently.
questions.modelAnswer: TWAP (time-weighted average price) splits the order into equal-sized pieces and submits one piece at each of several evenly spaced time intervals, regardless of how much volume is actually trading at any given moment. VWAP (volume-weighted average price) instead sizes each slice proportional to the market's typical trading volume at that time of day, trading more when the market is naturally busier (and can absorb more size with less impact) and less when it's quiet. Both approaches aim at the same underlying goal — getting the full order filled near the market's natural average price over the execution window rather than paying the full cost of dumping the whole order into the book at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: TWAP is the simple one: equal slices, equal time gaps, done. VWAP is smarter but needs more infrastructure: it has to estimate (or react to) the expected volume curve throughout the day and size slices against that curve instead of against the clock.
questions.example: For a 13,000-share order over a trading day split into 13 equal time windows, TWAP sends exactly 1,000 shares in each window; VWAP might send 3,000 shares in the first window (heavy open volume) and only 700 shares in a quiet midday window, sizing each slice to that window's share of the day's expected volume.
commonMistakes: Describing TWAP and VWAP as the same thing with different names
Not identifying volume-proportional sizing as VWAP's distinguishing feature
Missing that TWAP's simplicity is also its weakness (it ignores liquidity conditions)
Confusing either algorithm with a limit order strategy
keyPoints: TWAP: equal-sized slices at equal time intervals, ignoring volume
VWAP: slices sized proportional to expected trading volume at each point in time
Both aim to reduce market impact versus trading the whole order at once
VWAP requires a volume forecast/profile; TWAP does not

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes TWAP's equal-time-slicing structure
Correctly describes VWAP's volume-proportional structure
States the shared goal of reducing market impact

questions.title: The Five Pieces Every Systematic Strategy Needs
questions.prompt: Someone says they have a 'trading strategy' that's really just an idea: 'buy stocks that have been going up.' What five components would that idea need to actually become a runnable, systematic strategy?
questions.modelAnswer: A systematic strategy needs five components fully specified: universe (which instruments are eligible, defined without hindsight), signal (the exact rule that turns data into a view on direction and attractiveness), position sizing (how much capital or risk a signal gets, given its strength and the available risk budget), risk rules (stop-losses, exposure caps, correlation limits that keep one bad bet from being catastrophic), and execution (how the signal actually becomes an order — timing, order type, and realistic trading cost). 'Buy stocks that have been going up' is an idea, not a strategy, because none of these five things are nailed down — if you can't turn it into an unambiguous rule a computer could execute without a human in the loop, it's a hunch, not a strategy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on calling that a strategy at all — it's a hunch until all five pieces are specified. Universe, signal, sizing, risk rules, execution. If any one of those is still vague, you don't have something you can actually backtest or run.
questions.example: A fully specified version might read: 'Universe: S&P 500 constituents, point-in-time. Signal: 12-month price momentum, cross-sectional rank. Sizing: top-decile stocks get equal risk-weighted positions. Risk rules: max 5% in any single name, stop review if portfolio drawdown exceeds 10%. Execution: VWAP over the first hour of trading, rebalanced monthly.'
commonMistakes: Treating a vague idea as already being a strategy
Naming only one or two of the five components instead of all five
Omitting execution, treating signal generation as the whole strategy
Not explaining why an unambiguous, computer-executable rule is the actual bar for 'strategy'
keyPoints: Universe: which instruments are eligible, defined without hindsight
Signal: the rule turning data into a directional view
Position sizing: how much capital/risk a signal gets
Risk rules: stop-losses, exposure caps, correlation limits
Execution: how the signal becomes an actual order

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names all five components
Explains why an idea without these isn't yet a strategy
Gives a concrete example of specifying at least one component

questions.title: Position Limits vs. Just Watching the P&L
questions.prompt: A desk head says 'we don't need hard position limits, we just watch the P&L closely.' What's the architectural gap in relying only on P&L monitoring, without explicit position or inventory limits?
questions.modelAnswer: P&L is a lagging signal — it tells you what has already happened to the value of a position, not how large or concentrated the underlying exposure actually is right now. A position can grow to a dangerously large size while P&L still looks fine, simply because the market hasn't moved against it yet; by the time P&L reflects a problem, the position itself may already be far larger than anyone intended. Explicit position and risk limits are a leading, structural control — they cap the size of the exposure itself, independent of whether the market has moved yet, which is a fundamentally different and complementary kind of protection than watching P&L after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: P&L tells you about damage that's already happened; position limits prevent the exposure from getting large enough to cause that damage in the first place. Those are two different layers of protection, and relying on only the lagging one means you find out about a problem after it's already baked in, not before.
questions.example: A position could grow from a small, intended size to ten times that size purely through accumulating fills, with P&L staying flat the whole time because the price hasn't moved — a position limit would have stopped the size from growing in the first place, while pure P&L monitoring would see nothing wrong until the price eventually does move.
commonMistakes: Agreeing that P&L monitoring alone is sufficient risk control
Not distinguishing between a lagging indicator (P&L) and a leading, structural control (position limits)
Missing that a position can grow large with no immediate P&L impact
Treating this as an either/or rather than explaining both controls are complementary
keyPoints: P&L is a lagging signal reflecting what has already happened to value
A position can grow large with no immediate P&L impact if the market hasn't moved yet
Position/inventory limits are a leading, structural control on exposure size itself
The two types of controls are complementary, not substitutes for each other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies P&L as a lagging indicator
Explains how a position can grow dangerously without P&L reflecting it yet
States that explicit position limits are a necessary, complementary control

questions.title: Alert or Kill Switch — Which One?
questions.prompt: Sort these three events into either 'should page a human but keep trading' or 'should trigger an automatic kill switch': (1) the daily loss limit is breached, (2) the data feed is running three minutes late, (3) an unusually large single trade executed but didn't breach any limit.
questions.modelAnswer: The daily loss limit breach belongs in the kill switch — it's a genuinely hard, pre-committed risk limit, and breaching it should automatically stop new orders (and often flatten positions) with no human judgment call involved. The data feed running late and the unusually large (but non-breaching) single trade both belong as alerts — softer warning signs that should notify a human promptly without automatically stopping the strategy, since an automatic stop has its own cost (missing a genuine opportunity, or badly timing an exit) that isn't justified for anomalies that haven't actually crossed a hard limit. Confusing these two categories in either direction — auto-stopping on every minor anomaly, or only ever alerting on genuinely hard limit breaches — both lead to real losses in practice.
questions.professionalAnswer: Only the hard, pre-committed limit breach goes in the kill switch — that's event 1. The other two are exactly the kind of softer anomaly that should page someone without auto-stopping anything, because stopping the strategy over a slightly late data feed or one big-but-not-limit-breaching trade has its own real cost.
questions.example: If every unusually large trade auto-triggered a kill switch, a strategy could be constantly, needlessly halted on completely normal, non-breaching activity — which is exactly the over-reaction failure mode this split is designed to avoid.
commonMistakes: Putting the late data feed or the large non-breaching trade into the automatic kill switch category
Treating all three events the same way instead of distinguishing hard limits from softer anomalies
Not recognizing that an automatic stop has its own real cost (missed opportunity, bad timing)
Suggesting the daily loss limit breach should only be an alert, not an automatic stop
keyPoints: Hard, pre-committed risk limit breaches (daily loss limit) belong in the kill switch
Softer anomalies (late data, a large-but-non-breaching trade) belong as human alerts
Auto-stopping on every minor anomaly is its own failure mode
Only ever alerting, never auto-stopping on genuinely hard limits, is the opposite failure mode

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sorts all three events into the right category
Explains why the hard limit belongs in the kill switch specifically
Explains the cost of auto-stopping on minor anomalies

questions.title: Margin Accounts and Daily Mark-to-Market
questions.prompt: Explain why futures contracts are marked to market daily, and what actually happens to a trader's margin account when the price moves against their position overnight.
questions.modelAnswer: A futures contract is marked to market daily: at the end of every trading day, the exchange calculates each side's gain or loss based on that day's price move and settles it in cash immediately, crediting or debiting each party's margin account — a deposit held with the broker as collateral. If the margin account's balance falls below a required maintenance level after a loss, the holder gets a margin call and must add more cash or have the position closed out. This daily cash settlement is specifically what makes futures so much safer for the clearinghouse to guarantee: nobody's loss is ever allowed to build up unchecked for months the way it can on a forward contract, which settles only once at expiration.
questions.professionalAnswer: Daily mark-to-market is the mechanism that keeps a clearinghouse comfortable guaranteeing every futures trade — losses get settled in cash every single day instead of silently accumulating until expiration. If your margin account can't absorb another day like that, you get a margin call before the loss has a chance to grow into something the system can't handle.
questions.example: If a trader is long a futures contract and the price falls $2 in a day, their margin account is debited by $2 per unit that evening; if that debit pushes the account below the maintenance margin level, a margin call follows immediately, not at expiration.
commonMistakes: Confusing futures' daily mark-to-market with a forward contract's single settlement at expiration
Not explaining why daily settlement makes futures safer for the clearinghouse to guarantee
Describing a margin call as optional rather than a required response to falling below maintenance margin
Missing that gains are also credited daily, not just losses debited
keyPoints: Futures are marked to market daily; forwards settle once at expiration
Daily gains/losses are settled in cash into/out of the margin account
Falling below maintenance margin triggers a margin call
This prevents losses from building up unchecked, which is why futures are safer for a CCP to guarantee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the daily mark-to-market mechanism
Correctly explains the margin call trigger
Explains why this makes futures safer than forwards for the clearing system

questions.title: Why the Strategy Shouldn't Know Which Broker It's Talking To
questions.prompt: A firm's trading strategy code directly calls broker-specific API functions throughout its logic. What architectural problem does this create, and what layer should sit between the strategy and the broker instead?
questions.modelAnswer: Mixing broker-specific calls directly into the strategy logic means any change to broker, protocol, or venue requires rewriting the strategy's own signal and risk code — a completely unnecessary coupling between 'what to trade' and 'how to physically route it.' The right layer is an order management system (OMS): a stable internal interface the strategy calls (submit order, cancel, check status), which translates those calls to whatever protocol a specific broker actually speaks underneath — REST, FIX, or a native API. This means the strategy code never needs to know or care which protocol is underneath, and adding a second broker or switching venues doesn't require touching the strategy's trading logic at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The strategy should only ever talk to a stable internal interface — submit, cancel, check status — and have no idea whether that translates to a REST call, a FIX session, or something else entirely underneath. The moment strategy logic and broker plumbing are tangled together, adding a second broker or switching venues becomes a rewrite of the trading logic itself, which is exactly the kind of unnecessary coupling good architecture avoids.
questions.example: An OMS exposing a single `submit_order(symbol, qty, side)` method lets the same strategy code run unmodified whether it's connected to a REST-based retail broker or a FIX-based institutional venue — only the OMS's internal translation layer changes.
commonMistakes: Not identifying the unnecessary coupling between strategy logic and broker protocol as the core problem
Proposing to just duplicate the strategy code for each broker instead of introducing an abstraction layer
Not naming the order management system (OMS) concept specifically
Missing that this coupling makes adding a second broker or venue far harder than it needs to be
keyPoints: Mixing broker-specific calls into strategy logic creates unnecessary coupling
An order management system (OMS) should sit between strategy logic and the broker
The strategy calls a stable internal interface regardless of underlying protocol
This makes adding a second broker or switching venues far easier

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the coupling problem
Proposes an OMS-style abstraction layer as the fix
Explains the practical benefit (easier to add brokers/venues)

questions.title: Tell Me About a Time You Cut a Losing Position
questions.prompt: Walk me through a time — in a trading simulation, a class project, personal trading, or any comparable decision — where you had to cut a losing position or decision rather than let it ride, hoping it would come back.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names a specific situation, states the predetermined rule or threshold that triggered the exit (rather than a gut feeling decided in the moment), describes the actual decision to cut the position even though there was a real temptation to wait for a recovery, and reflects honestly on the outcome — whether the cut turned out to be the right call in hindsight or not, and what that taught about the value of deciding exit rules in advance rather than in the heat of the moment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through a specific case, name the rule I'd set beforehand, and be honest about how tempting it was to just wait one more day. The part that actually matters to an interviewer isn't whether the trade worked out — it's whether I had a pre-committed rule and actually followed it instead of negotiating with myself in the moment.
questions.example: A candidate might describe setting a stop-loss level before entering a position, watching the price approach it while feeling the urge to move the stop further away 'just this once,' and ultimately honoring the original rule and exiting — even though it was uncomfortable.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague, generic answer with no specific situation or number attached
Describing a decision made purely on gut feel in the moment, with no pre-set rule
Only describing a case where the cut worked out well, avoiding any genuine reflection on uncertainty
Framing the question as purely about the outcome rather than the decision process
keyPoints: A specific, concrete situation, not a generic description
A pre-committed rule or threshold, decided before the pressure hit
Honest reflection on the temptation to avoid cutting the loss
Focus on the decision process, not just whether the outcome was good

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides a specific, concrete example
Describes a pre-committed rule or threshold rather than a purely gut decision
Reflects honestly on the difficulty and the outcome

questions.title: Handling an Unexpected Large Loss Day
questions.prompt: You've just had a trading day that lost far more than any normal day in your recent history. How would you handle the next hour, and what would you actually do differently going forward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the immediate reaction from the longer-term response: in the first hour, the priority is following any pre-committed risk rules exactly (respecting the kill switch or loss limit rather than trying to 'trade back' the loss), communicating clearly and promptly with whoever needs to know, and not making any new large decisions while emotionally compromised. Afterward, the right response is a calm review of what actually happened — was this a known, expected tail event within the strategy's normal risk profile, or a sign something is genuinely broken — rather than an immediate overreaction in either direction (ignoring it, or abandoning a sound approach after one bad day).
questions.professionalAnswer: The first hour is about discipline, not analysis — follow whatever the pre-set rule says, don't try to immediately win it back, and tell the people who need to know. The actual analysis of whether this was a normal tail event or a real problem comes afterward, with a clear head, not in the same hour the loss happened.
questions.example: A disciplined response might mean honoring an already-breached daily loss limit by stopping trading for the day exactly as designed, reporting the loss to a risk manager promptly, and scheduling a calm post-mortem review the next day rather than an emotional one immediately after the loss.
commonMistakes: Describing an impulse to immediately trade more aggressively to 'win back' the loss
Not separating the immediate disciplined response from the later analytical review
Failing to mention communicating the loss to relevant stakeholders promptly
Overreacting by suggesting the entire strategy should be abandoned without any actual review
keyPoints: Immediate priority: follow pre-committed rules, don't try to trade back the loss
Communicate promptly and clearly with whoever needs to know
Separate the immediate disciplined reaction from the later calm analysis
Avoid both ignoring the loss and overreacting by abandoning a sound approach

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a disciplined immediate response rather than an emotional one
Mentions prompt communication with relevant stakeholders
Separates immediate response from later calm review and avoids overreaction

questions.title: A Decision Made Under Time Pressure With Incomplete Information
questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to make a real decision quickly, without all the information you would have liked to have. What did you actually do, and how did you think about the risk of being wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific decision, acknowledges explicitly what information was missing at the time rather than pretending the decision was made with full confidence, explains the reasoning process used to decide anyway (a quick cost-benefit framing, a default to the more conservative option, or a pre-set rule for exactly this kind of ambiguous situation), and reflects on whether that process — not just the outcome — was sound given what was actually knowable in the moment.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest version of this story always includes 'here's what I didn't know yet' — pretending otherwise is a red flag to anyone who's actually traded. What I want to show is that I had a sensible way of deciding anyway: lean conservative when the downside of being wrong is asymmetric, and don't let the search for more information become its own form of inaction.
questions.example: A candidate might describe needing to decide whether to reduce a position size before a data release with ambiguous signals, choosing the more conservative reduction because the downside of being wrong at full size clearly outweighed the upside of being wrong at a smaller size.
commonMistakes: Claiming the decision was made with full information, undermining the premise of the question
Describing indecision or excessive delay rather than an actual timely decision
Focusing only on the outcome and skipping the reasoning process used under uncertainty
Giving a hypothetical rather than a real, specific example
keyPoints: Explicitly acknowledges what was unknown at decision time
Describes a concrete reasoning process for deciding despite the gap
Shows awareness of asymmetric downside when uncertain
Reflects on the soundness of the process, not just the outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides a specific, real example with genuine missing information
Describes a sound reasoning process for deciding under that uncertainty
Reflects honestly on the process rather than just the result

questions.title: Telling a Risk Manager You Made a Mistake
questions.prompt: You realize you placed a position significantly larger than you intended, and it's already resulted in a modest loss. How do you communicate this to the risk manager, and what do you actually say?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer prioritizes speed and directness: report the mistake immediately rather than waiting or hoping it resolves itself, state exactly what happened in concrete terms (the intended size, the actual size, the current exposure and loss), and propose a clear next step rather than just delivering bad news with no plan. It should avoid minimizing the mistake or being defensive, since a risk culture that punishes honest, prompt disclosure more than it punishes the underlying mistake itself quietly trains people to hide problems — exactly the outcome good risk communication is meant to prevent.
questions.professionalAnswer: Speed matters more than how polished the explanation sounds — I'd go straight to the risk manager, say exactly what happened in plain numbers, and come with a proposed next step rather than just handing them a problem. Being defensive or minimizing it is the one thing that actually erodes trust here, more than the mistake itself usually does.
questions.example: 'I intended to size this position at 2% of risk budget and it's actually sitting at 6% due to an error in my sizing calculation — current loss is $X. I'd like to reduce it back to the intended size now unless you want to handle it differently.'
commonMistakes: Delaying disclosure in the hope the position recovers before anyone notices
Being vague or minimizing the size of the actual error
Reporting the problem with no proposed next step at all
Becoming defensive rather than focusing on clear, factual communication

State exactly what happened in concrete, specific terms
Propose a clear next step, don't just deliver the problem
Avoid defensiveness or minimizing — prompt honesty should be the safer choice, not the riskier one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Emphasizes prompt, direct disclosure
Describes communicating specific, concrete facts
Proposes a clear next step rather than just reporting the problem

questions.title: Why Trading Over Research or Development?
questions.prompt: What's actually different about a quant trader's day-to-day compared to a quant researcher's or a quant developer's? Why does that difference appeal to you specifically?
questions.modelAnswer: A quant researcher designs and backtests trading signals and models, leaning heaviest on statistics and often handing off a signal rather than trading it directly. A quant developer builds and maintains the infrastructure — data pipelines, backtesting frameworks, execution systems — leaning heaviest on software engineering. A quant trader executes strategies and manages risk in real time: deciding how and when to enter and exit, managing intraday limits, and reacting to live market conditions, needing market intuition and decisiveness on top of enough technical fluency to understand the models being traded. A strong answer connects a genuine personal preference — enjoying live, time-pressured decision-making over originating a model from scratch or building systems — to this specific distinction, rather than giving a generic 'I like markets' answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest distinction is originating versus running: researchers originate the idea, developers build what runs it, and traders are the ones making the real-time call once it's live. What pulls me toward trading specifically is the immediacy — I'd rather be the person deciding in the moment than the person who handed off a model and found out how it did three months later.
questions.example: A researcher might spend weeks validating whether a signal has genuine, persistent edge; a trader using that same signal spends their day deciding exactly when to act on it given live market conditions, position limits, and what's happening in the book right now.

Describing the trader role as requiring no technical skill at all
Not connecting the distinction to an actual personal preference or self-reflection
Confusing trading with research by describing model-building as the main daily activity
keyPoints: Quant researcher: designs and backtests signals/models, statistics-heavy
Quant developer: builds and maintains trading/research infrastructure, engineering-heavy
Quant trader: executes and manages real-time risk, market-intuition-and-decisiveness-heavy
A strong answer connects this distinction to a genuine personal preference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the three roles

questions.title: Reversing a View Quickly When You're Wrong
questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had a strong view about something — a trade, an analysis, a plan — and new information came in showing you were wrong. How quickly did you actually change your mind, and what made that hard?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names the original view honestly (without retroactively softening how confident it actually was), describes the specific new information that contradicted it, and is candid about the psychological difficulty of reversing — the sunk-cost pull to keep defending a position already taken — rather than claiming the reversal was effortless. It should end with what was actually done: concretely changing the position or decision, not just privately admitting the original view was wrong while continuing to act on it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part people tend to leave out of this story is how uncomfortable it actually felt — I'd rather admit that the sunk-cost pull was real than pretend reversing was easy. What matters is that I actually changed the position once the evidence was clear, not just that I privately conceded the point.
questions.example: A candidate might describe holding a bullish view on a trade, then seeing a clear piece of disconfirming data, honestly admitting the discomfort of abandoning a thesis already acted on, and describing the concrete action taken (reducing or closing the position) rather than just an internal change of opinion.
commonMistakes: Claiming the reversal was easy or immediate with no real internal resistance
Describing only a change of private opinion without any corresponding change in action
Giving a vague example with no specific new information that triggered the reversal
Framing the original view as never having been strongly held in the first place, undermining the premise
keyPoints: Names the original view honestly, including real confidence in it
Identifies the specific new information that contradicted it
Is candid about the psychological difficulty of reversing
Describes a concrete change in action, not just a private change of opinion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides a specific, honest example of holding a strong view
Candidly describes the difficulty of reversing
Describes a concrete resulting action, not just a private opinion change

questions.title: Staying Disciplined Through a Losing Streak
questions.prompt: You've had five losing days in a row on a strategy you still believe is sound. How do you keep yourself disciplined during that stretch, rather than either panicking and shutting it down or stubbornly ignoring real warning signs?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer leans on pre-committed, objective checks rather than in-the-moment feelings: did the losing streak actually breach any pre-set risk limit or statistical threshold, or is five losing days within the normal, expected range of noise for this strategy's known volatility? The discipline comes from having decided in advance what would actually justify concern (a specific drawdown level, a specific number of consecutive below-threshold periods) rather than reacting to the emotional discomfort of the streak itself. It should also acknowledge genuinely checking for a real problem — not dismissing every losing streak as 'just noise' by default — while resisting the urge to abandon a sound process purely because of short-term pain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The discipline isn't 'ignore the losses' and it isn't 'panic at the first bad stretch' — it's having decided in advance exactly what would actually justify concern, and checking honestly against that bar instead of against how uncomfortable the streak feels. Five losing days might be completely normal noise for one strategy and a real red flag for another; the pre-set threshold is what tells you which one this is.
questions.example: If a strategy's historical worst streak within its normal range is seven losing days, a five-day streak is likely within normal variation and shouldn't trigger a shutdown — but the same five-day streak on a strategy whose historical worst streak was three days would be a genuine signal worth investigating.
commonMistakes: Describing pure willpower or 'staying positive' rather than an objective, pre-set check
Dismissing every losing streak as noise by default, without genuinely checking for a real problem
Describing an immediate shutdown purely based on emotional discomfort
Not referencing the strategy's own historical baseline to judge whether the streak is actually unusual
keyPoints: Lean on pre-committed, objective thresholds rather than in-the-moment feelings
Check the streak against the strategy's own known historical range of normal variation
Genuinely investigate for a real problem rather than dismissing all streaks as noise
Avoid both premature shutdown and stubborn denial of real warning signs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes using pre-committed, objective thresholds rather than gut feel
Shows genuine openness to checking for a real problem, not blind dismissal
Avoids both overreaction and denial as failure modes

questions.title: Monitoring Your Own Emotional State While Trading
questions.prompt: How do you actually check whether your own emotional state is affecting your trading decisions in the moment, rather than realizing it only after the fact?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names concrete, specific habits rather than a vague 'I try to stay calm' — examples include noticing when a decision is being made faster than usual or outside a normal process (a sign of emotional urgency overriding discipline), checking whether a trade is being justified with a story that wasn't part of the original plan (a sign of after-the-fact rationalization), or deliberately pausing before any decision made shortly after a large loss or gain, since both extremes tend to distort judgment. The key is describing a real, repeatable check rather than just asserting good emotional control as a trait.
questions.professionalAnswer: I look for specific tells rather than trusting a general feeling of being fine: am I about to act outside my normal process, and am I justifying this with reasoning that wasn't part of the original plan? Both are better predictors of an emotionally driven decision than how calm I think I am in the moment.
questions.example: A trader might set a personal rule to pause for five minutes and write down the actual reasoning before acting on any trade that comes immediately after a large loss — specifically because that's the moment emotional decision-making is most likely to override discipline.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague, trait-based answer ('I'm naturally calm under pressure') with no concrete mechanism
Claiming perfect emotional control with no acknowledgment that it's genuinely difficult
Describing a check that only happens after the fact rather than in the moment
Not giving any specific, repeatable habit or process
keyPoints: Concrete, repeatable habits rather than a vague claim of good emotional control
Noticing decisions made outside the normal process as a warning sign
Watching for post-hoc rationalization that wasn't part of the original plan
Deliberately pausing after large wins or losses, both of which distort judgment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a concrete, specific, repeatable check
Shows genuine self-awareness rather than an overconfident claim
Mentions that both large losses and large gains can distort judgment

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Senior Trader
questions.prompt: A senior trader on your desk wants to hold a position you believe should be cut, based on something specific you've noticed. How do you raise the disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes raising the disagreement directly and promptly rather than staying silent or going around the senior trader, stating the specific observation driving the concern in concrete terms rather than a vague unease, and framing it as a question or a shared risk rather than an accusation — while being genuinely open to being told something the junior person doesn't know yet. It should also acknowledge that after raising the concern clearly once, respecting the final call (assuming it doesn't cross a hard, pre-committed risk limit) is part of functioning on a real desk, rather than repeatedly re-litigating the same disagreement.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd raise it directly, right away, with the specific thing I noticed rather than a vague feeling — 'here's exactly what I'm seeing and why it concerns me' — and frame it as a question, since there's a real chance they know something I don't. Once I've said it clearly, if it doesn't breach a hard limit, I respect the call; the goal is making sure the concern was heard, not winning the argument.
questions.example: 'I'm seeing the correlation between our long and short legs breaking down faster than usual in this move — is that something you've already accounted for, or should we revisit the size here?' is a concrete, specific, non-accusatory way to raise exactly this kind of disagreement.
commonMistakes: Staying silent to avoid conflict rather than raising a genuine, specific concern
Framing the disagreement as an accusation rather than a shared question
Giving a vague, non-specific concern instead of naming exactly what was observed
Describing repeatedly re-litigating the decision after it's been raised and addressed once
keyPoints: Raise the disagreement directly and promptly, not silently or indirectly
State the specific observation in concrete terms, not a vague feeling
Frame it as a question, genuinely open to being wrong
Respect the final call after raising it clearly, barring a hard limit breach

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes raising the concern directly and specifically
Frames the disagreement respectfully and non-confrontationally
Shows appropriate deference to the final call, barring a hard limit issue

questions.title: What 'Edge' Means to You
questions.prompt: People throw around the word 'edge' constantly in trading. In your own words, what does it actually mean, and how would you know if you genuinely had it, versus just having had a lucky run?
questions.modelAnswer: Edge is the structural or informational reason a strategy's return should persist — not the historical return number itself. A strong answer explains that a positive historical result alone doesn't prove edge exists, since it could equally be a statistical fluke from a finite sample; legitimate sources of edge include processing public information faster or more completely than others, being willing to hold risk others want to offload, or exploiting a structural friction that persists because fixing it isn't worth it for most participants. Knowing you have real edge, rather than a lucky run, requires being able to articulate why the pattern should keep working going forward, and being honest that a single good result is a claim, not proof.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd define edge as the answer to 'why would this keep working,' not 'did this work in the past.' A good track record and a real edge can look identical for a while, and the only honest way to tell them apart is being able to name the actual structural or informational reason behind the result — if I can't name that reason, I treat the result as unproven, no matter how good it looks.
questions.example: 'I bought stocks that went up last month and made money' describes a result, not edge. 'I'm faster at processing a specific kind of public information than most other participants, so I consistently act on it before the price fully reflects it' describes an actual source of edge.
commonMistakes: Defining edge as simply 'a strategy that made money'
Treating a good backtest result as proof of edge rather than a claim that needs a structural explanation
Being unable to name any specific legitimate source of edge
Showing overconfidence rather than genuine humility about distinguishing skill from luck
keyPoints: Edge is the structural/informational reason a result should persist, not the result itself
A positive historical return can be luck, not edge
Legitimate sources: faster/better information processing, willingness to hold unwanted risk, exploiting a persistent friction
Being unable to name the actual reason behind a result means edge is unproven, not confirmed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes edge (the reason) from a result (the outcome)
Names at least one legitimate, specific source of edge
Shows genuine humility about distinguishing skill from luck
